1:
The chapter opens on a date, and the witnesses spend most of their comment establishing that it is not the date it appears to be. The reformed John Gill argues that "the day that Moses had fully set up the tabernacle" cannot be the day the structure was first reared, since that fell on the first day of the first month in Israel's second year out of Egypt, whereas the princes' offerings — and a good deal else recorded in the preceding chapters — came after the first day of the second month. Nor can it be one particular day at all, he adds, since the princes were twelve days successively bringing their gifts. "The day" marks a season rather than a date: the time when the tabernacle was not merely put together but fully set up, everything in its proper place and order.

John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, reads it the same way and gives the sequence that fixes it. Day here stands for time, and the events belong to the second month of the second year, after the tabernacle and altar and all their instruments had been anointed, after the Levites had been separated to their service and appointed to their several works, after the numbering of the people at which these very princes were first constituted, and after the tribes had been disposed about the tabernacle — the order of which encampment, he notes, is exactly the order kept in the offerings. Adam Clarke dates the transactions to the second day of the second month of the second year, and holds that the proper place of the account is immediately after the tenth chapter of Leviticus.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, draws a rule from the timing rather than a chronology. The presents did not begin until everything commanded had been done, both about the tabernacle itself and about the camp surrounding it: necessary observances must always take place of free-will offerings — first those, and then these. He is equally interested in who came forward. The princes of Israel, heads of the house of their fathers, went before the rest, and Henry thinks that is what rank is for. Those advanced above others ought to go before them, and try to go beyond them, in everything that is good; the more a man is advanced the more is expected of him, since wealth and authority are good for little except the greater opportunity they give of serving God and one's generation.

John Calvin, reformed, adds two cautions. The first is about the givers: although only the princes are mentioned, no private man at that time was wealthy enough to give so much gold and silver of his own, so each is to be understood as presenting in the name and at the desire of his whole tribe what its members had subscribed. The second is about the anointing. Moses, who was not anointed himself, anointed both the sanctuary and his brother — proof, Calvin says, that the efficacy of consecration did not come from the man, since he could not give of his own what he did not possess. The whole virtue and use of the signs depends on the command of God, who institutes nothing in vain, but fills what he typifies with the secret influence of the Spirit.
2:
What the princes bring first is not gold but transport: six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two princes and an ox for each, presented before the LORD and set down before the tabernacle. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, treat this as the earliest event in the chapter and spend their comment on the one word that is genuinely uncertain in it. The Septuagint renders the phrase as lampenic wagons, which the Greek scholiasts gloss as a conspicuous or royal vehicle, a covered carriage; Aquila and the Vulgate give simply covered wagons, and Eusebius of Emesa took them for two-wheeled vehicles. The rendering "litters," which Gesenius and De Wette support, they reject outright as defensible neither on etymology nor from the one other place the word occurs.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, is blunter about the same crux: no one pretends to know what a lampenic chariot was, and "covered" or "tilted" is probably what the original means. He and John Wesley agree on the purpose — the heavier parts of the tabernacle could not conveniently be carried on men's shoulders, and the wagons made their transport both easier and safer.

John Calvin, reformed, presses the covering itself. The wagons were tilted so that what was laid in them should not be exposed to the rain, and he reports Ainsworth's suggestion that the Hebrew word derives from the shell that covers a tortoise. A yoke of oxen to each wagon settles the rest: these were vehicles for the materials of the tabernacle on the march, not conveyances for men. He notices too that the gift is made "before the LORD" and then "before the tabernacle," and refuses to read a difference into the two phrases, since God had as it were put on that face in which he might be beheld by believers.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, observes what the timing of the gift implies. No sooner is the tabernacle fully set up than provision is made for taking it down again — even when we are just settled in the world and think we are beginning to take root, we must be preparing for removes. He also notes that no pattern of these wagons had been shown to Moses in the mount, and they were not refused for that: the divine institution of ordinances does not descend to every circumstance that human prudence may fitly determine, that wisdom which is profitable to direct (Titus 1:5). And these were the same princes who had already given precious stones when the tabernacle was framing (Exodus 35:27); those who have done good, Henry says, should abound in it yet more, and not grow weary of well-doing.
4:
The gift is not simply accepted; it is commanded to be accepted. The reformed John Gill takes the LORD's word to Moses as spoken out of the tabernacle, before which the wagons and oxen were standing, and reads "take it of them" as the divine verdict on a freewill offering: by this it appears that what the princes had done was according to God's mind and will, that they had been influenced and guided to it by his Spirit, and that it was well pleasing and acceptable in his sight. The offering was voluntary on their side and approved on his.

John Calvin, reformed, presses the tense of the sentence and gets a different sequence out of it. Where others render it "the LORD said unto Moses," as though Moses had not been ordered to receive the gift until it had actually been presented, Calvin renders it as a pluperfect — the LORD had spoken — and takes God to have required this tribute of the people beforehand. On that reading the princes were not improvising a generosity that God then ratified; they were answering a demand already made. He says plainly that he has chosen the pluperfect for that reason, and not because the Hebrew forces it — the choice follows from what he thinks the narrative requires, that a tribute of this size was asked for before it was brought. Calvin adds a supporting observation in the same direction: the number of the wagons looks calculated rather than accidental, fitted to what they would have to carry, which is easier to explain if the requirement came first.

The command that follows governs the whole distribution: the wagons and oxen are to be given to the Levites, to every man according to his service. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, gloss the phrase as meaning that Moses handed them over to the different classes of Levites in the measure their respective duties required. Adam Clarke and John Wesley, both wesleyan-arminian, say the same thing from opposite ends — distribute them as the Levites may need them, giving most to those with the heaviest burdens to bear; more or fewer, as the nature of the service and of the things to be carried required. The rule is need, not equality, and the next four verses apply it.
6:
Moses divides the twelve oxen and six wagons in a proportion that looks uneven until the loads are weighed. Two wagons and four oxen go to the Gershonites, four wagons and eight oxen to the Merarites, and to the Kohathites nothing at all. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, explains each share from the inventory of what the family carried. The Gershonites had the curtains, coverings and hangings — a cumbersome carriage that needed wagons but was not a heavy one. The Merarites had the boards, bars, pillars and sockets, so they received twice as many. The Kohathites had the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, and those were to be carried on the shoulder; such sacred things, Clarke says, must not be drawn by beasts. John Wesley puts the same reason positively: on their shoulders, because of the greater worth and holiness of the things they carried.

Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, give the same division and add two details from the surrounding law — that the Merarites' work was under the hand of Ithamar, and that the holy things the Kohathites bore had been provided with poles for exactly this purpose.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, does the arithmetic that makes the arrangement vivid. Even with four wagons the Merarites can hardly have carried everything in them: the silver sockets alone weighed a hundred talents, above four tons, which would load four wagons drawn by a yoke of oxen apiece. Since a talent is about a man's burden, he supposes they shouldered the sockets and put the boards and pillars into the wagons. What he draws from it is a principle about strength and work: God wisely and graciously ordered the most help to those who had the most to do, each having wagons according to his service — and whatever burden God's providence lays on us, his sufficient grace will proportion the strength to it (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Henry also reads the Kohathites' empty hands as a standing rule rather than a hardship, and points to what came of ignoring it. In David's time the ark was carried in a cart, and the death of Uzza taught Israel to their terror that they had not sought the Lord in the due order (1 Chronicles 15:13). The reformed John Gill notes only that Moses took the wagons and the oxen as he had been directed, and that what went to Merari was all that remained.
10:
The altar had already been sanctified when it was anointed; what happens now is something else. The reformed John Gill describes it as the altar of burnt offering being set apart to sacred use — or rather, having been sanctified, now beginning to be made use of for sacrifice. John Wesley draws the distinction sharply: this is not the first dedication of the altar and the altar of incense, for both had been consecrated already by Moses and Aaron, but a further dedication, these being the first offerings made for any particular persons or tribes. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, puts it in a homelier word — the altars were now handselled by the princes with their freewill offerings, their use begun with rich presents and great expressions of joy.

Henry lingers on what was brought and what it was for. Twelve large silver dishes of about sixty ounces and as many silver bowls of about thirty-five: the dishes for the meat offerings and the flesh of the sacrifices, the bowls for the drink offerings and the blood. This was God's table, as it were, and it was fit that so great a King should be served in plate; the golden spoons, filled with incense, were probably for the golden altar, since both altars were anointed at the same time. In works of piety and charity, Henry says, we ought to be generous according to our ability — he that is best should be served with the best we have. Israel could well afford it, needing neither to buy food, being fed daily from heaven, nor to buy land or pay an army, being shortly to be put in possession of Canaan.

John Calvin, reformed, works out the same vessels by weight and use: the sacred cakes were received in the dishes, the wine of libation in the bowls, and the frankincense in the censers, and God would have each tribe contribute its own set so that the common interest of the whole people in the sacrifices might be the better testified. His attempt to price them runs into the difficulty that the shekel of the sanctuary was double the common one, and he ends by leaving one point undecided — whether there were gold shekels as well as silver — rather than pretending to a knowledge he has not got.

Then the LORD settles the manner of it: each prince on his day. Gill notes that until this word came Moses did not know how they should offer — whether by birth order or by the order of the camps, whether together or one after another. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, and John Wesley both answer that the sequence followed the camp rather than birth. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, adds that every prince offered on behalf, and doubtless at the expense, of his whole tribe; and Calvin thinks the spreading of the gifts over twelve days was itself devotional, a lengthened exercise by which even careless hearts might be stirred up.
12:
Judah gives first, and John Calvin, reformed, hears an oracle behind the arrangement. The sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10): the time had not yet come for that word to be proved by its fulfilment, but God so ordered matters that certain marks of supremacy already attached to the tribe, and by general consent, if not dominion, at least the chief dignity was always lodged there. Giving the first day to Nahshon was therefore a presage of the kingdom that would at length be set up in David. The reformed John Gill notes the plainer reason alongside it — Judah's standard was pitched first, on the east, toward the rising sun.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, notices something in how the prince is named. Nahshon alone of the twelve is not expressly called a prince, and Henry passes on the Jewish explanation that the title was withheld so that the man who offered first should not be puffed up, while the others, some of them of the elder house, are all called princes because they submitted and offered after him. He adds a second reading he plainly prefers: that the title prince of Judah belonged more properly to Christ, unto whom shall the gathering of the people be — Judah first and then the rest, as in the dedication of souls to God every man is presented in his own order, Christ the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:23).

The gift itself is then set out piece by piece, and the witnesses identify each object. The charger, on Adam Clarke's reading, is a deep dish in which the paste was kneaded; the bowl is a basin for receiving the blood of the sacrifice; the golden spoon is a censer on which the incense was laid. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, adds that the charger was for use about the altar of burnt offering or in the court, not in the sanctuary, whose vessels were all of gold. Gill reckons the spoon's ten shekels at four ounces, one drachm and nine grains, worth about seven pounds ten shillings in his own money, and takes the bullock to be three years old on the authority of the Targums.

Every kind of offering is present at once, and Gill makes the point explicitly: meat and drink offerings, burnt offerings, a sin offering and peace offerings, all in a single day's gift. Wesley explains why the peace offerings are the most numerous of them — the princes, the priests and some of the people made a feast before the LORD out of them, so the quantity answers to the number that had to eat.
18:
Issachar follows Judah, and the second gift is the first repeated without a variation. Nethaneel the son of Zuar brings the same silver charger and silver bowl, both full of fine flour mingled with oil; the same golden spoon of ten shekels full of incense; the same bullock, ram and lamb of the first year for a burnt offering; the same kid of the goats for a sin offering; and the same two oxen, five rams, five he goats and five lambs for the peace offerings.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, points out what is governing the sequence, and it is not seniority. The princes come forward in exactly the order in which their tribes were encamped about the tabernacle. Judah, Issachar and Zebulun stood together on the east side under one standard, and they give on the first three days in that order; the southern, western and northern camps will follow in their turn, each keeping its own internal order as it kept it in the camp and on the march. Nothing is being settled here about the comparative dignity of the tribes. The arrangement God had already made for Israel's marching is simply carried across into the arrangement for Israel's giving, so that a man who knew where his tent stood knew when his prince would offer.

Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, read the sequence the same way, noting that the order of presentation answered to the order of the tribes in the camp, with Judah's prince leading and Naphtali's coming last.
24:
The east side of the camp finishes with Zebulun on the third day, Eliab the son of Helon bringing the same vessels and the same beasts as the two princes before him.

John Calvin, reformed, explains why these three tribes come together at the head of the twelve, and the answer turns on a family relation rather than on rank. Zebulun and Issachar were ranked under Judah's banner in the camp, so they march with him and they give with him. Both were sons of Leah, and both were younger than Judah, who was her fourth; the two who follow him here are the two who came after him in the household. Calvin uses the point to defuse an objection he expects: it looks like a slight that the tribes should be ordered this way at all, but the order is neither arbitrary nor a ranking of worth. Israel was divided into four divisions of three, and every division's leader draws the tribes set under him along with him.

The gift itself repeats the first day exactly — charger and bowl, the golden spoon of incense, the three beasts of the burnt offering, the kid, and the peace offerings — and with Eliab's day a quarter of the dedication is complete. The standard that had led the camp eastward toward the sunrise has now led the giving as well, and the offering turns south.
30:
With the fourth day the offering crosses to the south side of the camp, and the prince who comes forward is Elizur the son of Shedeur, of Reuben — the firstborn of Jacob's sons, waiting until three younger tribes have gone before him.

John Calvin, reformed, raises that as an objection against his own account of the order and then answers it. If the sequence follows the camp rather than birth, is it not absurd that Reuben, the eldest, should be kept back to the fourth day? The answer is that Reuben has not been demoted but given a division. Israel's twelve tribes were arranged as four divisions of three, and the fourth day is the first day of the second division: Reuben comes at the head of Simeon and Gad, with two tribes attached to him, and Calvin judges this the more honourable place of the two. To lead a camp is worth more than to be third in another man's.

The gift itself is unchanged — charger, bowl, spoon, bullock, ram, lamb, kid, and the two oxen and three fives of the peace offering — and Reuben brings neither more for his seniority nor less for his delay. Calvin's reading is borne out by the sameness: the tribes differ in their place, and not at all in what they bring.
36:
Simeon offers on the fifth day, Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai bringing the second of the three gifts that come from the southern camp.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, takes up here the fact that will not stop being true for the rest of the chapter: all the offerings are exactly the same, without any variation. He does not think the twelve princes were equally rich, nor the twelve tribes equally able; some of these gifts, he suspects, were made up by contribution from the tribe rather than out of one man's estate. That the sums came out identical is therefore a decision, not an accident. What it signified was that all the tribes of Israel had an equal share in the altar and an equal interest in the sacrifices offered upon it. One tribe was posted more honourably in the camp than another, but the tribes and their services were all alike acceptable to God.

Henry turns the point on the reader before leaving it. If the altar admitted no respect of persons, neither may the church: we must not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect to persons (James 2:1). Simeon's day is the plainest illustration of it, since nothing whatever distinguishes his gift from Judah's except the name at the head of it.
42:
Gad closes the southern camp on the sixth day, Eliasaph the son of Deuel offering what the five before him had offered.

By this point a reader has met the same inventory six times, and Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, asks the question directly: since the gifts were all the same, would it not have served to say of this noble jury that each brought what their foreman brought? He answers that God would have it specified for each tribe, and gives two reasons. The first is for the princes and their tribes themselves. Each of their offerings is recorded at length, so that no slight might seem to be put upon any of them — rich and poor meet together before God, and none of the twelve is summarised away.

The second reason reaches past Israel. Henry takes the repetition as an encouragement to every generous act of piety and charity, because what is so given is lent to the Lord, and he records it carefully with the giver's name set against his gift. He is not unrighteous to forget the work and labour of love (Hebrews 6:10); Christ sat over against the treasury and watched what was cast in (Mark 12:41). Though a gift be small, and though it be only a share in the charity of others, if it is according to our ability it is written down — and written down, Henry says, to be recompensed at the resurrection of the just.
48:
The seventh day brings the western camp forward, beginning with Ephraim: Elishama the son of Ammihud offers the charger and the bowl, the spoon of incense, the beasts for the burnt offering and the sin offering, and the peace offerings.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, reports that both Jewish and Christian writers have been troubled by this particular day, on the supposition that the seventh of the twelve must have fallen on a sabbath and that the work went forward on it regardless. His reply comes in two parts. First, there is no proof that this seventh day of offering was a sabbath at all; the sequence began when it began, and nothing in the record fixes it to the week. Second, and more to the point, even if it were, the objection assumes that what was being done was ordinary work. It was not. Every act here was a religious act, and Clarke will not allow that any day could be too holy for men to consecrate themselves and their service to the Lord on it.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, had reached the same conclusion by a shorter route: one sabbath at least must have fallen inside the twelve days, and it does not appear that they broke off for it, since this was holy work and proper enough for a holy day.
54:
Manasseh offers on the eighth day, Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur bringing the second gift of the western camp — and, as with every prince before him, a gift identical to the first.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, reads the sameness as a statement about debt. Every tribe offers the same kind of offering and in the same quantity because every tribe was equally indebted to God for its support, and each was therefore to testify an equal sense of obligation. What was brought is as deliberate as how much. The vessels were sacrificial vessels and the animals were clean animals, such as were fit for sacrifice and nothing else; the fine flour and oil for the meat offering, the bullock, ram and lamb for the burnt offering, the kid for the sin offering and the beasts for the peace offering are each of them appointed things, not gifts chosen for their value.

The whole was meant, on Clarke's reading, to point in one direction: that this was to be a holy people, fully dedicated to God, and that God was to dwell among them. As the priests and the altar had been anointed and the tabernacle set apart, so the people by this offering were consecrated too — which is why he insists that every act in these twelve days was a religious act rather than a civic one.
60:
Benjamin ends the western camp on the ninth day, Abidan the son of Gideoni offering as the others have offered.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, closes his account of these gifts by handing the last word to Ainsworth, whose reading looks straight through the inventory to what it stood for. By sacrifices of all sorts, figuring the death of Christ and the benefits that were to be received by it, the offerers reconciled themselves and made themselves and theirs acceptable to God; they were made partakers of his grace to the remission of sins and to sanctification through faith and in the work of the Holy Ghost; and in the communion and feeling of that grace they rejoiced before God.

The remark is worth making at this day rather than another, because the completeness of the list is Ainsworth's ground. It is not the burnt offering alone, nor the sin offering alone, that Abidan brings. He brings the meat offering, the incense, the burnt offering, the sin offering and the peace offering together, and so does every prince: the whole range of the sacrifices at once, twelve times over. What is figured is correspondingly whole — reconciliation, dedication and communion in a single day's gift, which is why the rejoicing Ainsworth speaks of belongs to the same act as the kid of the goats.
66:
The tenth day opens the northern camp with Dan, whose prince Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai brings the vessels and the beasts in their fixed order — and among them, as on every other day, one kid of the goats for a sin offering.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, will not let that item pass unnoticed, and it is the one thing in the list that might have been thought out of place. This was a time of joy and rejoicing: the altar was being handselled, the peace offerings were to be feasted on with friends, and the whole twelve days were a festival. Yet in the midst of these sacrifices a sin offering stands, day after day, unchanged.

Henry draws the lesson without softening it. Since in our best services we are conscious to ourselves that there is a mixture of sin, it is fit that there should be even in our most joyful services a mixture of repentance. The princes were not confessing that the dedication was insincere; they were confessing that they were sinners while they made it. And Henry turns the kid of the goats forward: in all our approaches to God we must by faith have an eye to Christ as the great sin offering, and make mention of him. The gift Dan brings on the tenth day says the same thing the first day said, and says it with the same small animal.
72:
Asher offers on the eleventh day, Pagiel the son of Ocran bringing the same charger of a hundred and thirty shekels and bowl of seventy, the same golden spoon of incense, the same three beasts for the burnt offering, the same kid, and the same peace offerings. The reformed John Gill sets the prince down with his father and his tribe as the record has it, the second of the three princes of the northern camp.

What holds Adam Clarke's attention here is not the offering but the way the day is counted. The Hebrew, he observes, has something curious in it: where the English says simply "the eleventh day," the original runs beyom ashtey asar yom — in the day, the first and tenth day — and again at the head of the twelfth day beyom sheneym asar yom, in the day, two and tenth day. Set out like that, the phrase looks laboured to an English eye, as though the writer were spelling out on his fingers what a single word ought to carry.

Clarke's point is that the strangeness runs in both directions, and the wesleyan-arminian commentator turns the criticism back on English before anyone can level it at Hebrew. Our own numerals are the odder pair. From thirteen upward the composition is transparent — thirteen is three and ten, fourteen is four and ten — but eleven and twelve bear almost no analogy to ten and one and ten and two, which is nevertheless exactly what they mean. To a Hebrew reader, he suggests, our anomalous words would look as peculiar as his construction looks to us, and the Hebrew at least has the merit of saying what it means on its face.

He then sets the observation down where it belongs, calling it a matter of philology rather than of biblical criticism — a note on how a language counts, not a difficulty in the text. Nothing in the sense of the verse is at stake, and Pagiel's gift is entered exactly as the ten before it were entered. Asher's turn falls where it does for the reason every turn falls where it does: on Clarke's own reckoning of the camp, Asher stood on the north side between Dan and Naphtali, so the eleventh day is his exactly as the tenth had been Dan's and the twelfth would be Naphtali's.
78:
The twelfth and last day belongs to Naphtali, and Ahira the son of Enan brings what the eleven princes before him had brought. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, note only that the order which began with the prince of Judah ends here with the prince of Naphtali, exactly as the camp was arranged; Adam Clarke observes that the Hebrew counts this day as it counted the last, in the day, two and tenth day.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, gathers up what the twelve days were for. God appointed that the offerings should be brought on separate days so that the solemnity might be prolonged and universally noticed by all Israel, and the memory of it the more effectually preserved. It also gave an equal honour to every tribe: as each had his own precious stone in Aaron's breastplate, so here each had his own day. And it kept the thing orderly — God's work should not be done confusedly or in a hurry.

Henry adds two reasons a reader might not have looked for. The priests and Levites, offering the same sacrifices of every sort twelve days running, would have their hands well set in and would come to know the laws concerning them thoroughly. And the peace offerings had to be eaten the same day they were offered; two oxen, five rams, five he goats and five lambs were enough for one day's festival, and had all twelve gifts come at once there might have been danger of excess. The virtue of temperance, Henry says, must not be lost under pretence of the religion of feasting. With Ahira's gift the last of the twelve days closes.
84:
The account closes by adding everything up, and the totals are worth having in one place: twelve silver chargers of a hundred and thirty shekels each and twelve silver bowls of seventy, two thousand four hundred shekels of silver in all; twelve golden spoons of ten shekels apiece, a hundred and twenty shekels of gold; twelve bullocks, twelve rams, twelve lambs and twelve kids for the burnt and sin offerings; and for the peace offerings twenty-four bullocks with sixty rams, sixty he goats and sixty lambs.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, takes the opening phrase carefully. "In the day when it was anointed" cannot mean a single day, since each tribe had a whole day for its prince to present what it had provided, so the dedication necessarily ran to twelve; the words point to the last of them, the twelfth, on which the whole was completed. He also glosses the closing formula "after that it was anointed" as the note of consecration — by the anointing the altar was set apart to God, and by this dedication it was solemnly appointed to the service for which it had been erected. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, reads the same phrase as the chapter's own correction of itself: it explains in what sense the dedication is repeatedly said to have happened on the day of the anointing, namely in a latitude — a little after it, not exactly on it.

The reformed John Gill goes through the sums as they stand. These were the presents made and the offerings offered when the altar first began to be used, after it had been anointed and sanctified. The twelve golden spoons full of incense point at what such cups were for; the twelve bullocks of the burnt offering answer to the number of the princes and their tribes; the twenty-four of the peace offerings work out at two from each prince. Wesley notices one item that appears only here — the meat offering, mentioned in the total though not in any of the twelve individual accounts, and left out of them, he judges, because the law that required it made it sufficiently understood.
89:
The twelve days end and Moses goes in, and what happens inside is the chapter's real conclusion. The reformed John Gill supposes he went in to consult God on some affair, or to learn whether there was anything further to be delivered to the children of Israel, or perhaps about the princes' gifts themselves, since this follows immediately on their offerings. What he heard was a voice speaking to him from off the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that overshadowed it. Gill will not take that voice for the Father's, since no man has heard his voice at any time (John 5:37); he takes it for the voice of the Shechinah, the eternal Word who in the fulness of time was to be made flesh and dwell among men, and be heard and seen and handled by them.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, reaches the same conclusion by a different road. Moses saw no similitude and heard only a voice, yet had the fullest proof of God's presence and being; this was how God chose to manifest himself under that dispensation, until the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Clarke draws out the name of the place. Because God gave oracular answers from the mercy seat, it was called the debir, the speaking place, from the verb to speak — so that the incarnate Christ is the true oracle in and by whom God now speaks to men, as the writer to the Hebrews says God has in these last days spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, says the same in a sentence, and adds why the verse stands where it does: when men had done their part, God was not wanting in the performance of his.

John Calvin, reformed, faces an apparent contradiction instead. Elsewhere a thick cloud stood in the door of the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter; here he enters and is answered. Calvin's solution is chronological rather than harmonising: Moses sought God's replies at the mercy seat until Aaron began to exercise the priesthood, and then gave up that temporary dignity, since by God's established law the priesthood was distinct from the civil government and one man could not be both leader and priest except by special privilege. On that reading the verse is not recording something that happened after the offerings but stating, at the end of the narrative, what had been true throughout. Its purpose, he says, was to declare to posterity that God had not promised in vain that Israel should experience the presence of his favour — and by this testimony of grace the external anointing was itself ratified.
